t.3.44.1: But Rāghava's younger brother, addressed harshly by her, was angered; intensely longing for Rāma, he set out almost at once.
t.3.44.2: Then the ten-necked Daśagrīva, seizing the opportunity, swiftly took his stand in that opening and, wearing the guise of a wandering mendicant, approached Vaidehī.
t.3.44.3: Clad in smooth ochre robes, wearing a topknot, carrying a parasol and wearing sandals, and then hanging a staff and a water-pot on his fair left shoulder, he approached Vaidehī in the guise of a wandering ascetic.
t.3.44.4: The exceedingly mighty one approached her, left alone in the forest without the two brothers, as the deepest darkness approaches twilight bereft of both sun and moon.
t.3.44.5: Then he, exceedingly dreadful like a malign planet, beheld that young and illustrious princess, who was like Rohiṇī bereft of the moon.
t.3.44.6: Seeing that fierce doer of evil deeds, the trees growing in Janasthāna do not stir, and the wind does not blow.
t.3.44.7: And the swift-flowing river Godāvarī, seeing him gazing about with red eyes, began out of fear to flow sluggishly.
t.3.44.8: But the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, seeking an opening against Rāma, in that interval approached Vaidehī in the guise of a mendicant.
t.3.44.9: The ill-intentioned one, wearing a pleasing form, approached Vaidehī as she grieved for her husband, just as Śanaiścara approaches the star Citrā.
t.3.44.10: That sinful one, concealed beneath a pleasing form like a well covered over with grass, stood there gazing at Vaidehī, the illustrious wife of Rāma.
t.3.44.11: The lovely lady with beautiful teeth and lips, her face like the full moon, seated in the leaf hut, tormented by tears and grief.
t.3.44.12: That night-roaming demon, wicked of heart, approached Vaidehī, whose eyes were like lotus petals and who was clad in yellow silk.
t.3.44.13: Pierced by the arrows of Manmatha, the lord of the rākṣasas, intoning Vedic recitation, spoke courteous words to her in that lonely place.
t.3.44.14: Rāvaṇa praised her, the most excellent woman of the three worlds, who shone with her beauty like Śrī without her lotus.
t.3.44.15: Who are you, O lady with the radiance of gold, clad in yellow silk, wearing a lovely garland of lotuses like a lotus pond?
t.3.44.16: Are you Hrī, Śrī, Kīrti, or auspicious Lakṣmī, or perhaps an apsaras, O fair-faced one? Are you Bhūti, O lady of lovely hips, or Rati wandering at your own free will?
t.3.44.17: Your teeth are even, pointed, smooth and white; your eyes are large and clear, reddish at the corners, with dark pupils.
t.3.44.18: Your hips are broad and full, and these two thighs, like the trunks of elephants, are plump, rounded, close together, and splendidly firm.
t.3.44.19: Your breasts are lovely and beautiful, full with upraised tips, like smooth palm fruits, and adorned with ornaments of the finest jewels.
t.3.44.20: O you of lovely smile, lovely teeth and lovely eyes, O graceful and charming woman, you carry away my heart as the water carries away a riverbank.
t.3.44.21: Your waist could be spanned by a hand; you have lovely hair and full, close-set breasts. Surely you are no goddess, no Gandharvī, no Yakṣī, nor a Kiṃnarī.
t.3.44.22: Never before on the face of the earth have I seen a woman of such form; this, and your dwelling here in the wilderness, drive my mind to madness.
t.3.44.23: Turn back, may good fortune be yours; you ought not to dwell here. This is the abode of the fearsome rākṣasas, who take on whatever form they wish.
t.3.44.24: The finest of palaces and the delightful gardens of the city, richly furnished and fragrant, are fit to be frequented by you.
t.3.44.25: Excellent is the garland, excellent the drink, and excellent the garment, O lovely one; and excellent too, I deem, is the husband who is joined with you, O dark-eyed lady.
t.3.44.26: Who are you among the Rudras or the Maruts, O you of pure smile, or among the Vasus, O lovely-hipped one? You appear to me to be a goddess.
t.3.44.27: Neither gandharvas nor gods nor kiṃnaras come here; this is the dwelling of rākṣasas. How then have you come here?
t.3.44.29: O lovely-faced lady, how is it that you, all alone in this great forest, do not fear the fierce and mighty elephants maddened with rut?
t.3.44.28: Here there are monkeys and lions, and likewise leopards, tigers and deer, bears, hyenas and herons; how is it that you are not afraid of them?
t.3.44.30: Who are you, whose are you, and from where have you come, O lovely lady? For what reason do you wander alone through the dreadful Daṇḍaka forests frequented by rākṣasas?
t.3.44.31: Thus was Vaidehī praised by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa. Seeing that Rāvaṇa arrived in the guise of a twice-born, Maithilī honored him with all the courtesies due to a guest.
t.3.44.32: First bringing him a seat and welcoming him with water for washing his feet, she then said to that one of gentle appearance, "It is ready."
t.3.44.33: Maithilī, seeing him arrive in the guise of a twice-born, bearing a bowl and a water-pot, found it impossible to turn him away because of the outward form he presented, and so she invited him, just as he had come, as one would a brahmin.
t.3.44.34: Here is a seat, O brāhmaṇa; please sit as you wish, and accept this water for washing your feet. And this excellent food, prepared from what grows in the forest, is for you; enjoy it here at your ease.
t.3.44.35: Invited by Maithilī, the wife of the lord of men, who spoke to him with full courtesy, Rāvaṇa gazed at her and laughed, and he gave over his mind, now set on carrying her off, to his own destruction.
t.3.44.36: Then, as she waited for her finely attired husband, who had gone hunting with Lakṣmaṇa, and gazed all around, she saw only that vast green forest, but not Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
